blocks.x: I'll make a note that we're recording an interview with Mr. Sam Dutre at 731 St. Peter Street. This is Bill Russell interviewing, and the date is April the 14th, 1962. Do you mind giving your full name, Mr. Dutre?
Oh, Samuel O'Donnell Dutre, Jr.
You're named after your famous father.
My father, yes, right.
Can you tell us your birth date, if you don't mind? Exactly. My birth date. My birth date. My birth date.
My birth date. Born 1909.
1909. Where were you born? Right here in the city?
In the city of New Orleans, on Lower Line Street.
On Lower Line?
Right, Uptown.
Oh, that's Uptown.
Yes.
Uptown. Can you tell us the earliest music you remember? Was it in your home? Do you remember hearing your father play in practice? Anything that you can think of about your father, we'll talk about.
I was quite a while back. I was a kid. And they used to have a club in the neighborhood where I was staying. It's called the Buffaloes Club. And I heard my father play there for the first time.
And it was Uptown?
Yes, Uptown 17-Watt. And as for the band, I really couldn't say the band because I was very smart.

Yes, I understand. I wonder if you could give us a little information about your father, if you remember how old he was and when he died, so we can figure out just about his birth date. Do you remember when he was born or any of the facts about his life that way?

Well, I couldn't say too much about that because we never could voice on that. But from what I heard, he first came to New Orleans and bought him a pressing shop. And after which he went to the barber. And he began playing music with different outfits in New Orleans.
He worked as the barber in the press?
In a presser. That's been quite a while back then.

Yes, certainly I understand. When you were a kid, you weren't interested in all those things, so you wouldn't be interested in trying to remember it at that time. And now, of course, we're interested in all that oldest history that we can find about the musicians because the whole world, as you know, considers it important now. I wonder, do you remember the date of his death?
I really have forgotten that.

I had some notes here I'd gotten from somebody that I don't know if they were accurate. It said 1941. Do you think that would be right at the beginning of the war? Can you remember? Just about the time.
It's about 1941. We got into the war.
We got into, you know, Pearl Harbor. It was 1941, December.
It was 40 or 41. About that time.
Do you remember how old he was?
Well, no, I couldn't say.
Also, I was going to ask a little bit about your uncles. You had two uncles that played music. I understand, was it Peter was the violin?
Peter was the violin and the honoree was the drum on us.
How do you pronounce that? Honoree?
Honoree.
Honoree. Because I know Baby Dodds in Chicago who worked with him always called him Nora.
That was a nickname. Yeah, Norae.
Norae. And is there anything else you can tell us about your father? Do you remember who he might have? Did he ever say where he learned music or when he learned it?
Well, no. They never discussed that in front of me. They kind of picked it up and I don't know. I couldn't say.
I know you just took it for granted that they'd always played music.
Well, yes.
Can you remember some of the bands that he worked in?
Well, that's funny. The only band I do remember is Amos Raleigh marching band.
Yes.
A parade band.
Out on the street.
No. We didn't discuss. I mean, as a kid, I didn't discuss who he was working with. Who was working with, yeah. But I do remember he was working out on the lake there.
Oh, did he play up until his death about or did he retire from music?
Oh, he retired and went back to Baldwin.
He didn't? He didn't play then at the very end. You didn't hear him then in the lake years. No, I didn't. You remember about the last time you might have heard your father?
Oh, the last time I heard him play was the Union had a ball up on the Pithin Temple. Yes. And he was playing flute in that band.

Well, he played flute too. I didn't know that. Yes, he did. The only flute player, piccolo, really, was Bab Frank that I ever heard of in the old days that he played flute and jazz. He played a regular, a long flute then.
He played piccolo flute. He was practically all around me.
I know he played sax too. Do you know which sax he played?
Alto.
The alto. Did he ever play Kenner or any of the others?
Well, I don't know. But he first started with a C melody.
C melody. Oh, yeah.
And then he changed to alto.
Do you remember when he started? Was it during your time that you can remember when you were a boy?
I remember him coming to the house with a C melody. He played some that day. And that was all I heard of it until next time I saw him head out there.
Alto, yeah. Is there anything else about your uncle? He was younger than your father, wasn't he?
Yes, he was the youngest brother.
He was the youngest brother.
Yeah, Peter was the oldest and my father in between.
Andre was the youngest. You mentioned that you had been up to Chicago once and saw your uncle there?

Well, yes. During the, it was the First World War. He passed through here. He had to go to the dentist and save his teeth. Fixed. And he went to Chicago and I didn't see him for quite a while. He came down here on the excursion and then he went back. And the next time I saw him, I went up on a boat with Sidney Desvane.
Who is?
And I passed through there and saw him. That was in 1933. 1933. But when I finished high school, he gave me vacation up there. I started when I was 23.
Do you remember who he was working with in Chicago at that time?
Oh, yes. King Oliver.
King Oliver.
Louis Armstrong, Baby Dodds, Lil, and I think they had a Jackson on the banjo.
Oh, yes. Some Jackson.
And Johnny Dodds playing Granite.
Yeah. I wonder if you can tell us about your earliest days now in music when you started out. How old were you and what instrument did you start on?
I started on the clarinet.
Right on the clarinet? Yeah, I started on clarinet.
Well, during my time coming up, you would go up to a place and the fellow would say, Oh, boy, go home and let me ask you to kind of think about it. Yeah.
I've heard how they did that.
Well, the first fellow, that was very rare. The first fellow who gave me a chance to play a little was George Lewis. He was playing with René at the time.
And he said, go ahead, play, have your fun. I said, okay.
I played a couple numbers. I was so elated.
Did you have any regular lessons? Did your father, anyone?
Oh, my father taught me.
That's what I thought of you.
He taught me. And so we got into it. I didn't bring a lesson one day. And he and I had it. So I stopped going. And from then on, from then, I went on more.

Professor Mineta, you know, who played with you the other night, claims that he learned all he knows, mostly about clarinet from your father, that he was a wonderful teacher. And he's told us what a wonderful musician he was. Probably so.
And I didn't know that he had, well, they were friends until here of late, you know.

Yes. He always talks about Sam Dutre and, of course, the younger brother, too. But mainly Sam, he'll talk about being such a, sometimes Emmanuel would have a band downtown here. And your father would come and sit in. And some of those people downtown thought they were better musicians than the ones uptown. Oh, yeah.
That was the time back then.

Professor Mineta said, though, your father always showed him up. And they could read the stuff better than they could do it, really. Oh, yeah. Did he make you have a book when you started? Do you remember what book you had, method book and all?
I think it was Arturo Langley.
Oh, yes. Professor Mineta still uses that.
He does? Yes.
And he tells about that he learned from your father to cover both lips. Do you do that? I never did notice when you played.

Well, my father taught me that way. I had to start that way. Do you still do that? No, I don't. You don't do that now? No. And after I got able to play some, he said, well, you don't have to cover each other teeth anymore.
Mm-hmm. Very few people do it. I think Barney Bigard does that.
He does.
He's about the only one that I've seen of the jazz musicians.
It's all right. But I think it's best that you start that way because you have more lip control. Now, if you just start with your teeth up there, I don't think you have too much power, lip control.
Well, did you start on the Albert system or Bain or Huchard?

Albert. On the old Albert. I stayed on the Albert. Never the change. Well, there wasn't any printing changing because I can play both systems, but I just wanted to show the fellas that you could get as much out of an Albert that you could do with a Bain.
Yeah. And most of the New Orleans fellas, almost all of them used it.
I guess. Yes, they did at the time when they came out, they started changing.

Yeah. Still, a lot of them used it. People like Edmund Hall and of course the fellas around here almost all use the Albert system too. Did you notice much difference in the two systems? In the tone, if there's any difference in tone? I know the keys are a little easier on the Bain.

There isn't any difference in the tone. The tone comes from the man. The only thing, the systems are not too much a part. B flat, B natural, F and F sharp, C and C sharp. Yeah. That's the only difference on this.

I wonder if there's much difference like in the bore or something. If some people told me the Albert system maybe is a little bit more, a bigger bore inside. And maybe some people think they can get a bigger tone now, the Albert. I wondered if you'd ever noticed anything like that.
Well, I have noticed that. But I seem to get the same tone from both instruments.
I should think most people would. Do you remember anything else about your lessons as your father?

Oh, well, during the time he was working out there at Southwood. Not Southwood. Moonbury. Out on the lake. Yeah. Oh, well, he'd tell me to come to the lesson. I'd say about three o'clock. And I'd have to wait around until about five or six and we would be sleeping. And if I didn't have that lesson, I'd have to start for me.

I've heard he's very strict. I know one of the last times I saw Louis Armstrong in Chicago. And I don't know how the question of your father came up. If he mentioned him first, he mentioned, I think, the first time he played on the boat. Your father was playing in the band. And Louis was always, he says, short now, you know how small he is. And he must have been real small when he was a kid, 18 or so. And your father was very, oh, I don't know, they say he was very strict and all anyway. And he saw this little kid getting on the stand of the coronet. And he said, what are you going to do, you know? And he said he scared Louis. He said he always was afraid of your father after that. He was sort of afraid of him. I mean, he knew he wasn't, he was a kind man. He wasn't trying to say that. But I mean, he was trying to, he was so strict about his music. And he scared Louis that first time when he was just a little kid. And he said he always was afraid of your father.
Well, I read it in the book that Louis put out. And he said it happened on the job when they were working down there, around Saratoga Street or somewhere.
Oh, yeah.
I heard it happened there when he said.

I think Louis told me it was on the boat the first time he comes. Louis could have said it slipped up on one time or otherwise. Otherwise, I say we've heard very little about your father, except things that Professor Minetta remembers him very well. And he took lessons from him, he said, and learned that Fess still plays that way on clarinet.
Yeah.

Covering both lips. Well, the teeth, I mean both upper and lower. And he always said that your father once pointed out, said go around and look at all the clarinet players and you'll see the ones that put their teeth on and have their teeth worn down there. Fess said, yeah, I went around and sure enough, some of them that, I think George Bakay and some of the others that did that, they had their teeth worn down their teeth. Did you ever have any trouble that way of actually wearing your teeth? Well, I don't know.
It may be, but I have noticed because I used the teeth up there, but I was very seldom on my teeth. Yeah. And that's why I say give you better lip control. Yeah.
The, oh, I was going to ask about sax, when you took up saxophone. Did you, how long did you play clarinet before you took up the sax?
Well, I couldn't, I can't recall that, but my father showed me the fingering and that's all.

He showed you the fingering on the saxophone too? Yeah, and that was all when I just started playing. Yeah. About how old were you when you started on clarinet? I was about eight. Eight? About eight. How long did your father give you lessons on the instrument, would you say, if you can guess about, I know it's hard to remember those dates and all exactly.
I can't recall the dates, but I must have been about eight or ten years.
Quite a while then, you worked with him. Yeah, maybe ten years. Yeah. Do you enjoy playing sax more or clarinet? What would you say?

Well, it doesn't matter. One is just like the other. You have to, but my father always would tell me, say, never put the clarinet down because you can have four off nights on your saxophone. They say the clarinet would keep you from having that.
Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. And so, I never did put it down. And sometimes I just, when I'm not working regularly, I just use the sax and pick up the clarinet and I think about what he said and I go back and get the method and start to work on it.

A lot of people I thought have told me that the saxophone seems a little bit easier to play. Do you think it's easier as far as the fingering goes? I mean, you don't have to cover the holes carefully.
Well, they can use to do anything with the saxophone and it'll come out, but you can't do that with the clarinet. Yeah, to be. A little harder to control.
Yeah. Paul, I think I would, again, your uncle, Peter, do you remember anything about him? Is he the oldest one? He was the oldest.

Older than your father. Yes, yes. Well, he, I was living with my grandmother and he came to stay with us and he stayed there quite a while. Well, at that particular time he was mostly a barber. He didn't play too regular. And he stayed in the profession until he died.
Now, do you remember about when he died? I know it's hard to bring up those dates and all.
Well, I wouldn't be able to tell you because I didn't put him down and I don't know.
But, he didn't live as long as your father, I guess. Did he? I don't, I never heard anything about him hardly until just four or five years ago that I've ever heard of him.
The only thing I can say that it was between 45 and 50. All three of the brothers died within that range. 45 and 50. But it was that age about. Yeah, yeah.

And he never played music then in late years. Do you remember who he might have worked with? Any bands that he might have played with? I can't say that. Did you ever hear him play at home or? Well, yes.

They, they, they used to have, they get together, my father and my uncle and, my uncle would play violin. And, my father would always say, well, you're supposed to play it like this. And, there was a discussion every time they get together.
Yeah. Did your uncle play any other instrument except the violin? Piccolo.
Piccolo.
Oh, the violin, uncle Peter had played the piccolo too. Piccolo. Mm-hmm. I didn't know that. Did he play in brass bands you suppose? Well, I don't know.
I can't.
Never did see him out on the street then.

No, I never did see Honoré or Peter. But, I do know that he played in a lot of the top brass bands like that. Yeah. I think it was Excelsior one band he played with before he left there. Yeah, I didn't even know. Because I had all the caps, he left me all the caps at the house. Well, he had the old caps.
Did you ever save those?
I saved them until my grandmother discovered them.

That's too bad he didn't save them, it'd be good for a museum or something. No, that's for sure. A lot of those old caps, people never see them again now. They have the names, I guess, on them. Yeah, they have the names.
Excelsior name.
It's way before my time.

They had three different caps. They had the regular film cap and they had the other cap with a white cap and they had another cap with a white band around it. I didn't know what that was for. As I was to now, I know they only carried two caps but he had three.
I was going to ask if you know anything else about your Uncle Peter, about how much older he was than your father? Could you try to guess at that? It's hard to tell. No, I can't.
You see, our family, we never did discuss anything. I mean, like that age. I know, most people wouldn't know those things.
Some people used to write them down in a Bible and things of that kind and they'd remember those dates, otherwise most people don't remember.
The only thing I probably could do is get them from my sister.
She probably had all that done.
Because Uncle Peter and my dad, they used to stay with my dad at times.
Is your sister older or younger than you?
She's younger.
Sometimes the women will take more interest in the family history than the men.
Oh, yes. She always did do that.

I'm wondering if you can tell us anything else about any other bands at all you can remember your father might have played in or jobs either where you heard him or heard where he was going or other men that came to the house to see him that might have practiced. Do you remember any other people he worked with?
Oh, he organized a band of his own.
He was the leader of the band.
Yeah, of his own band. The Silver Tone Orchestra. Silver...
Silver Tone.
Silver Tone. Yeah, I heard them, the hoists and I heard them play. But, as for the other bands, I really couldn't tell you because you never would say anything. And I was too afraid to ask.
Yeah, yeah. Do you remember who was in the Silver Tone? Anybody else that came there?
Peter Bocats. Oh, yeah.
Yeah. Peter playing the violin or trumpet? No, Peter Bocats.

No. He had a... Lance Moreira on a banjo. I think I get it wrong now. I say Peter Bocats. I have to come back to that. Oh, yeah. Yeah. And the Harrison Bones on Trump. Oh, yes. I knew him. He just died a couple years ago or less. Yeah. Babe on bass. Was that Phillips? Babe Phillips? Yeah, from Uptown.
Yeah. They called it sometime One-Eyed Baby. One-Eyed.
That's right. One-Eyed. That's right.
Yeah, I knew him. Yeah, I knew him.
Yeah, I knew him. Yeah, I knew him.
Yeah, I knew him. Yeah, I knew him. Yeah, I knew him. Yeah, I knew him. Yeah. In fact, we have a nice interview with him, too, before he got-
And I think he had one of the halls on the 10-Embrienton. I can't recall which one is that. I know he was on outdoor and another of a fellow they called.
Was that like Clarence Hall, that family of- The halls, yeah. Edmund Hall and Clarence Hall.
It was either of those. Yeah.
I can't think of the other brothers now, either.
I know. Well, I really, I can't recall him. I can see him right now, but I can't call him.

Yeah, well, anyway, that gives us some help on the- Mm-hm. Some of the fellows that were there. And I was gonna ask you then to get back to your life again. If you can tell us some of the very first job you had. You mentioned like sitting in, of course, with George Lewis and people of that kind. But the first job you ever got paid for, can you remember that?

Well, I was still going to school and we organized a little three piece outfit around the uptown, eh? Suddenly, this and Jerome Jerry Green, he was playing banjo and drum and I was playing clarinet. And the first job was opening up a drugstore. Oh, really?
Yeah. Used to have music for, they still do, sometimes when they open a restaurant or something. Oh, yeah.

And we used to, after we got known a little, Detective Lennice and Reagan used to hire us regularly for their little art and used to pay for them. Oh, yeah. And after that I think I went to Biloxi, Mississippi with Isaiah Morgan I think. And Sundoon, he's a New York man, he was a banjo player.
Who was that?
Sundoon.
I don't know.
That's in relation to Paul Barberand. He's a banjo player, he's a New York man. Oh, wait a minute. Barker. Oh yeah, sure.
Danny Barker.
Yeah, we called him Sundoon. Oh yeah, I never even knew anything.
Yeah.
He told Fess Jones and the fellas about me. And I started working with them, it was Lee Collins, Fess Jones, myself, Daniel Barker, Roy Evans, and Joe Rovershue.
Oh yeah. Most of those people, Lee Collins died about a year ago. Several of them are still around.
And then after that I used to do spotty jobs with Isaiah Morgan going in and out of town.
Yeah.
And then I worked the entertainers down here with Billy O'Connor. We went in there, Pessie Jones, myself, Roy Evans. It had a pretty nice little outfit in there.
Yeah, that was on the one up here on the Crozat Street or Franklin Street they used to call it. Yes. I remember the building but I never did get in there before then.
And after that I went with Sidney Desvien. Oh yes.
I played with them. Went on the boat with them.
On the boat and all too. And after that I went with Joe Rovershue. When was that?
Was that after the war started or before?
Oh, that was, you see, that was, I went with Desvien around 30, let's see, about 30, 30, one.
Way back in there then. That's why.
And I forgot one too.
You've been playing about 30, over 30 years now.
Oh, something like that. I had been, my father put me in luck when I was 12, that's been quite a while back then.
Oh really? Twelve years now?
That's right. And I played with B.B. Ridgely, Emmanuel Ridgely.
Oh yeah, we knew him, we got some interviews, we went to see him two or three times.
At the Hour Club, I played out there with them.
Yeah.
That's where I played with Emma Barrett, Gilbert Young, Mr. Harrison Bones, Maya Kennedy, and myself, and Jim Johnson. Yeah. That's been quite a while back then, 29. And then I went with Sidney.
How long did you stay with Sidney Desvien?
Oh, until the first part of 34. And then I went with Joe Robichaud. And stayed there until we changed the name of the band to John Lunsford.
See, were you on any of those records that Joe Robichaud made? I forget now.
Well I know he had a small outfit then. I forget that you were all known. Yeah, I know. I was quite a large man. There was Gene Porter, Gishard, Ransom Nolens, Eugene Ware, Bucket, and then Joe.
Yeah.
They were on the other record.
You see Bucket, who's he? What did he play? Drums. The drums.
He's in Chicago now. Yeah. He was from Chicago. I don't know his name. All I know is Bucket. I wasn't familiar with that either.
It was funny. And after Joe Robichaud, do you remember?
Oh yeah, we converted Joe Robichaud band into John Lunsford.
Oh, that's right.
And after we had to disband because we had too many young fellas. Knuckle Sam.
And the war came along then, huh? Yeah.
Knuckle Sam took him. And then we started on the Freddie Coleman band.
Oh yeah.
And after that, I'm freelancing. Yeah.
Oh, when did you move up? What's the name of the town? Opelousas?

Opelousas. Well, we opened a job there at the St. Andrew Club. I was in 43. I got married a couple years after. So I'm not glad to move there. Yeah. The wife didn't want to leave there. I did take her out on a couple of trips. And I know she wasn't satisfied and she started losing weight. So I say the best for me to take her back home and just branch off from there.
Is there much music up there?
Oh, there are a lot of bands, but a lot of rock and roll people. They go for that. The kids do, but the other people, they don't go out anymore like they used to.

Well, that's right. With the television and other things, most people stay home for their entertainment now, it looks like. I wondered, I thought maybe since you were up in that town that your family had come up that way, but your father and uncles never did come from there then. Well, I know. Do you know what part of the country they came? Or had they been, always right here in New Orleans?
Well, no, they came up from Pankalopee Parish and that's New Roads.
Oh, around New Roads.
Yes, that's right out of, about 20-something miles out of that.
Yeah, I never did hear where they came from.
Yeah, they asked where they came.
Any of the family still up there?
Well, I think so. That's another thing, my father never did take me out there. Yeah. But I played there a couple times and when I said do so, well, just looked like I was on the throne. Yeah.
Well, I think, were there any other, you only had the two uncles, your father, there were three brothers?
One died. He was a bass player, his name was Jimmy.
Well, he played bass.
Yeah, he died. I hadn't heard of him. Around 16.
Well, very young. Yeah.
It was way before my time, but I picked up that much.
You mean around, when he was 16?
No, 16 years of age. Oh, that's, I thought maybe 1916. Now, what brother and what, what the age limit I couldn't see.
Yeah.
But they said he was the youngest. Yeah, he was the youngest one. Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah, I hadn't known about him. Is there anything else about your life, the late years in music or anything else you'd like to add? I think that covers most of your lives. Yes, it's about, I don't know.
There isn't anything more I could say too much. I may think of something after I leave. I know it's always that way.
Yeah. The next day people say, well I should have told you about a certain band or something I did. But anyway, you can't think of everything.

But I played with practically everybody. I mean, I could say a lot of bands I played with, probably the Black Eagle bands of New Orleans. Oh yeah. I played with King Thomas, Kit Thomas from CrossFit. Oh yeah. I played with every band you have. Yeah, most people, most people usually say that too.
The New Orleans musicians would just change from one to another. They all played the same style mostly, so they could all switch from one band to another
easily. That's right.

Well, we certainly enjoyed talking to you and getting these facts and all as much as we could about your family and all too, because it's a famous name in music as everyone knows. I was going to, might ask a little bit, any other famous clarinetist that you remember hearing when you were a boy that you liked? Let's see.
You know, I was coming up, I tell you who I used to like the most, and that was the audition show.
I wondered if the old time fellas here, like say the Tio's, did you ever hear any of them, Lorenzo Tio? Lorenzo Tio.
Lorenzo Tio, but I didn't like him too well. Uh-uh.
Or Louie Nelson or Piqu and Bach Kay, any of those men? Some of those are left-handed.
George A. Boyd, George A. Boyd. Oh yeah. I mean, he, well they didn't class him as a clarinet, but I thought he could play more than all of those.
I know George Lewis talks about him being good and other people too.
I didn't think he could read it, but he could get over the instrument. And, uh, see that was Captain Hamley.
Oh yes, they tell me, he goes, he doesn't play clarinet part of the ending now, but he was one time they say he was great.
He was good, he was a good clarinetist. And that's about all. Oh yes, another fella, the one that died here. He said Miami was his name.
Who'd you play with?
The top clarinetist, the head here. I just can't recall his name now.
I can't think now who it was.
He had a, a trio on WWL. He was the best. He'd done with all those fellas out there, man. All those large names.
Yeah, I can't think now.
You can't think of the top clarinetist there?
Was he colored or white? Right. Or maybe Fazola.
That's it. Fazola, yeah. I admire him.
I used to hear it at the Bob Crosby band up in Chicago. Yeah, a nice tone, you know.
That's crazy right there. That's my tone.
Yeah, well, I think that covers everything fairly well, and we certainly, I'm glad I ran across you this morning to, so we could get this interview.
Well, I wanted you to have it.
It's been hard to catch you when you live out of town. I see. Okay, I guess we'll just turn it off. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
